Escudero bans phones, earpieces for impeachment trial witnesses. Presiding Officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero on Tuesday, Sept. 1, ordered all witnesses appearing before the Senate impeachment court to refrain from using cellphones, smartwatches, earpieces and other communication devices while testifying, citing the need to protect the integrity of the proceedings. Escudero issued the directive after an AI-generated image circulated online purporting to show former Office of the Vice President assistant secretary Lemuel Ortonio wearing an earpiece while testifying before the impeachment court. Escudero clarified that the image was not part of the official record and did not establish that Ortonio actually wore an earpiece or received outside assistance. “The Chair therefore makes no finding against him,” Escudero said. Nevertheless, he said the controversy underscored the need for a uniform safeguard against possible witness coaching, tampering, or outside influence. “Testimony must be the witness’s own and must remain free from tampering, coaching, or outside influence,” Escudero said. He cited the fundamental principle that witness testimony should remain free from coercion, coaching, or improper influence to preserve the integrity of judicial proceedings. Escudero also referred to US cases as persuasive authority, citing a 2003 Philippine Supreme Court ruling that foreign decisions may be considered persuasive when no local authority squarely addresses a particular situation. He cited the February 2026 US case Villarreal v. Texas, where Justice Samuel Alito, in a concurring opinion, said that when a defendant is testifying, defense counsel cannot pass notes to the witness or communicate with the witness through an earpiece. According to Escudero, Alito explained that a witness must provide his own account in his own words rather than testimony “scripted or choreographed by counsel.” Escudero likewise cited Sky Development, Inc. v. Vistaview Development, Inc., a 2010 US case that recognized that real-time coaching could come not only from lawyers but also from other interested persons through electronic messages. “The Court need not wait for actual coaching to occur,” Escudero said. “Once testimony is compromised, the harm to the truth-seeking process may be impossible to cure.” Under Escudero’s order, witnesses are prohibited from possessing, wearing, accessing or using any cellphone, smartwatch, earpiece, headset, smart glasses or other device capable of transmitting or receiving communications while testifying. Witnesses are also prohibited from receiving or attempting to receive any communication, suggestion, answer, signal, message, prompt, or assistance from any person, whether inside or outside the session hall. The restriction will also apply during recesses until the witness is formally discharged. Escudero ordered witnesses not to discuss the substance of their testimony with anyone during such recesses. Any medical, accessibility, interpretation, or evidentiary device deemed necessary, as well as consultations unrelated to the substance of the testimony, will require the prior approval of the presiding officer. The Clerk of the Impeachment Court was directed to inform every witness of the order, secure prohibited devices before witnesses are sworn in, and obtain their confirmation of compliance on the record. Any violation will be immediately reported to Escudero and may be dealt with under the impeachment court’s contempt and disciplinary powers.

Police capture gunman minutes after QC shooting. Police arrested a 32‑year‑old man on Sunday, Aug. 30, about 50 minutes after he allegedly shot a man four times while the latter was inside a tricycle on Samar Street in Barangay Alicia, Quezon City. The suspect, alias “Erd,” 32, of Barangay Santo Cristo, was arrested by Project 6 Police Station (PS 15) personnel at around 7:40 p.m. on Romblon Street in Barangay Santo Cristo. Police said the victim was inside a tricycle at around 6:50 p.m. when the suspect, armed with a gun, arrived on a motorcycle, got off, and fired four shots at him before fleeing. The victim suffered gunshot wounds and was brought by bystanders to Metro North Medical Center for medical treatment. Acting on information received, PS 15 personnel conducted a follow-up operation that led to the suspect’s arrest. At around 10:30 p.m., QCPD Scene of the Crime Operatives (SOCO) conducted a technical examination of the crime scene and recovered two fired cartridge cases and one fired bullet. The suspect is set to be charged with frustrated murder before the Quezon City Prosecutor’s Office. The Quezon City Police District, under Police Brigadier General Christopher Olazo, continues to investigate the circumstances and motive behind the shooting.

Leviste’s Solar Philippines unloads ₱3-billion SPNEC shares to anonymous investor, cuts stake to 11.5%. Leviste-led Solar Philippines Power Project Holdings Inc. (SPPPHI) has further pared its stake in SP New Energy Corp. (SPNEC), selling ₱3 billion worth of shares to an undisclosed buyer as founder Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste continues his corporate exit. In a disclosure to the Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE) on Tuesday, Sept. 1, SPNEC reported that SPPPHI sold approximately 2.4 billion common shares at ₱1.25 per share. The transaction reduced SPPPHI’s stake in the renewable energy (RE) firm to 11.51 percent from 16.3 percent. Although the statement blurred out the identity of the buyer, the purchase would allow the new owner to absorb another chunk of Leviste’s remaining holdings in SPNEC. Prior to this, Leviste had already resigned as a director of Terra Solar Philippines Inc. and SPNEC after the Department of Energy (DOE) sought to purge stalled RE projects earlier this year. SPNEC’s equity structure is currently led by Manuel V. Pangilinan-led MGEN Renewable Energy Inc. (MGreen) with a 57.33-percent controlling stake, followed by SPPPHI at 11.51 percent, also Pangilinan-led Metro Pacific Investments Corp. (MPIC) at 3.2 percent, and the remaining balance held by a new minority investor. Meanwhile, Meralco PowerGen Corp. (MGEN) approved a budget for the 280-megawatt (MW) Sta. Rosa solar project, even as financing details have yet to be shared with the public. “We are waiting for the DOE to allow us to proceed by granting our request to reinstate our service contract after showing that we have been developing it and faced challenges only in meeting the GEA [Green Energy Auction] timeline,” MGEN President and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Emmanuel Rubio told Manila Bulletin. To recall, the Sta. Rosa solar facility was among the numerous projects affected when the DOE canceled thousands of MW worth of RE service contracts linked to Leviste’s firm. MGEN is actively awaiting the DOE’s decision to allow it to pursue the project.

House probe eyed amid SOCOTECO II–Ignite Power controversy. A ranking House member is seeking a congressional inquiry on proposed joint venture between South Cotabato II Electric Cooperative Inc. (SOCOTECO II) and Ignite Power and Energy Corporation (Ignite). General Santos City lone district Rep. Shirlyn Bañas-Nograles, vice chairperson of the Committee on Nuclear Energy, introduced House Resolution (HR) No. 1401 for this purpose. Filed in the House of Representatives last Aug. 27, the measure directs the House Committee on Energy to conduct an investigation, in aid of legislation, into the Conditional Joint Venture Agreement (CJVA) between SOCOTECO II and Ignite. The resolution, pending first reading, seeks to determine whether the proposed arrangement complies with existing laws, rules and regulations, while examining issues of transparency, accountability and the prudent stewardship of cooperative assets. It also calls for an assessment of how the agreement could affect the rights and economic interests of the government and SOCOTECO II’s member-consumer-owners (MCOs). HR No. 1401 comes with "the end in view of determining compliance with existing laws, rules, and regulations; ensuring transparency, accountability, and the prudent stewardship of cooperative assets; protecting the rights and economic interests of the government and the member-consumer-owners; and strengthening the governance and regulation of joint venture arrangements involving electric cooperatives". Bañas-Nograles' initiative comes as opposition to the proposed partnership continues to grow. The Social Action Center of the Diocese of Marbel (SAC-Marbel) has raised questions regarding the process by which SOCOTECO II’s Board of Directors reportedly secured authority for the proposed joint venture. In a statement issued Aug. 20, the group alleged that Resolution No. 104 was declared adopted during the cooperative’s 43rd Annual General Membership Assembly on July 25 without a duly counted vote showing how many MCOs supported or rejected the measure. SAC-Marbel also questioned the use of a standing vote without an actual count and called for the deferment of the plebiscite, greater transparency and accountability, and an independent investigation into SOCOTECO II’s operations. The concerns have placed the proposed joint venture under greater public and regulatory attention, particularly on questions involving the management and long-term stewardship of electric cooperative assets. For businesses, consumers and other stakeholders within SOCOTECO II’s franchise area, the congressional inquiry could provide an avenue for greater clarity regarding the commercial, regulatory and governance implications of the proposed partnership. The House probe, if pursued, could become a significant step in determining whether the proposed partnership meets applicable legal and regulatory requirements and whether sufficient safeguards are in place to protect the interests of the cooperative and its consumers. Meanwhile, a peaceful candlelight rally opposing the joint venture was held on August 29 at Plaza Heneral Santos and along Pioneer Avenue. Protesters from municipalities within the Diocese of Marbel carried banners calling for the proposed deal to be stopped and for the protection of the rights, resources and interests of SOCOTECO II’s member-consumer-owners. The proposed plebiscite on the CJVA is scheduled over four weekends in September 2026.

Show evidence behind ‘wasted’ Lakeshore funds, Cayetano tells Lacson. Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano on Tuesday, September 1, continued to defend Taguig Lakeshore’s continued public use amid claims by Sen. Panfilo “Ping” Lacson that billions in government funds were wasted on flood control and infrastructure projects in the area. In a social media post on National Heroes Day, Cayetano insisted that under the management of Taguig City government, Lakeshore had not been neglected or wasted under pointing to its use for health, education, leisure, businesses, and other public functions. “Hindi po sinayang at hindi sinasayang ang Lakeshore (Lakeshore was not neglected or wasted). Let’s not let politics rob this generation and future generations of the opportunity to reap its benefits,” Cayetano said. Cayetano made the post after Lacson said P3.713-billion in completed, ongoing, and suspended DPWH projects within alleged reclamation areas in Taguig, may have been wasted. Earlier, Lacson also alleged other irregularities and said the findings would be submitted to the Office of the Ombudsman. Cayetano warned that this kind of partisan politics could derail efforts to address corruption and flood control, stressing the need for evidence-based investigations that lead to accountability. “The honest search for solutions is overshadowed by partisan politics. Corruption and flood control are perfect examples,” he said. The senator challenged Lacson that if there is any evidence against him, or the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) or the Taguig City government, he should present it. “If there is evidence against DPWH, Taguig, or against me, then present it. Stop the theatrics and let the evidence do the talking set in the proper judicial venue where fairness is assured,” he challenged Lacson. The lawmaker said the focus should remain on solving problems and ensuring that public funds and government efforts are directed toward projects and reforms that benefit Filipinos. “Every hour the government spends on political warfare instead of solving problems is wasted. Every peso spent on projects that do not serve the people is wasted. Every opportunity to reform a broken system sacrificed for personal or partisan advantage is wasted,” he said.

Hungary drained its waters for generations. Now drought is exposing the cost. GÁRDONY, Hungary (AP) — A fisherman disembarked from his boat in a small harbor on Lake Velence in Hungary last week, trudging up the dock plank that had become extremely steep as the water receded to record lows. Árpád Selmeci said that navigating even a small fishing boat on Hungary's third-largest lake is becoming increasingly difficult as the water level has ebbed to around 20 centimeters (8 inches), well below the 150 centimeters (5 feet) optimal for August. Swimming beaches across the lake, once popular with tourists, have been closed. Lake Velence’s decline is part of a broader water crisis confronting Hungary as increasingly prolonged droughts and climate change-driven heat waves have pummeled Europe. “I've lived on Lake Velence since I was a child, and I've never seen the water so low," said Selmeci, 58. "It's terrible. My heart aches every single moment.” This summer, wildfires scorched the continent from the United Kingdom to Greece, while in Hungary, drought has damaged crop yields, led to drinking water shortages and threatened to shut down the country's only nuclear power plant. Yet the lack of rainfall linked to human-driven climate change is only part of Hungary's water problem. Experts say the country's long-standing practice of channeling water away from its landscape and draining natural wetlands has left it especially vulnerable as droughts become more frequent and severe. A legacy of draining away water Around 99% of Hungary’s lands are currently under severe or extreme drought conditions, according to the national meteorological service, and desertification, a process where vegetation recedes because of high heat and low rainfall, threatens much of the Great Hungarian Plain. Yet more than a quarter of Hungary consists of low-lying land that naturally retains precipitation, and in past centuries its many rivers and streams made it rich in freshwater resources. However, a 2023 study published in the journal Nature estimated Hungary’s historical wetland loss at more than 80%. Zsuzsanna Ujj, a biodiversity policy specialist and project coordinator with environmental group Friends of the Earth Hungary, said the country “has not been a good steward of its waters in the last 200 years.” A major contributor is Hungary's network of more than 40,000 kilometers (25,000 miles) of drainage canals — a length that exceeds the circumference of the Earth — which drain accumulated precipitation from fields, wetlands and the soil to make room for agriculture and other enterprises. The priority on draining land rather than allowing natural flooding cycles to occur has contributed to a consistent drop in the water table and the drying out of wetlands and topsoil. With less water available to evaporate, the air dries out, further reducing the chances of localized precipitation. Ujj said that Hungary — which is among the most drought-exposed countries in Europe and ranks 16th globally, according to a report by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development — “needs to realign its water management practices, shifting from a drainage-based approach to one focused on water retention.” Disappearing lakes The drying out of Hungary isn't limited to streams and wetlands. Lake Garancsi, a small recreational lake around 20 kilometers (12 miles) northwest of Budapest, was once a popular destination for fishing, swimming and ice skating, and was the setting of the 2001 cult Hungarian comedy “Üvegtigris” (“Glass Tiger"). But the lake, present since the Middle Ages, has shrunk so dramatically in recent years that none of the previous recreational activities are permitted, and most of the former lake bed is now exposed, cracked and dry. What remains of the water is so shallow and warm that all of the fish and most of the other wildlife have disappeared, and authorities have predicted no water will be left by the end of summer. Zoltán Mettner, who runs the Glass Tiger bar on the shores of the lake, said conditions have gotten worse every year. After spending years beside the lake, he said looking at it now is “terrible, there’s no other way to put it.” “It’s sad enough that we’ve let things get this far, and that we couldn’t have taken gradual steps to prevent this lake from being completely destroyed,” he said. Hungary's government plans a change of course Hungary's new government has promised to begin taking those steps. In late June, on the same day the country set a high temperature record of 42 Celsius (107.6 Fahrenheit), Prime Minister Péter Magyar told lawmakers that his government would put water management policies “on new footing,” and launch a comprehensive water conservation program to mitigate the effects of drought. "Many have said year after year that water shortage will be one of Hungary’s problems and one of the most important strategic issues to be solved. They were right,” Magyar said. In addition to poor water retention practices, Magyar said that aging water utility infrastructure causes 20-25% of the country’s drinking water to leak out through damaged pipes, costing some 17 billion forints ($54.4 million) annually. “For years, even the existence of the problem was denied and relativized,” Magyar said. Now, he added, “water retention will be the basic principle of Hungarian water management.” Danube River at historic lows Yet implementing such sweeping changes will be time consuming and costly, while Hungary's current water crisis threatens its ability to produce adequate energy. The Danube, the European Union's longest river which runs through 10 countries from southwestern Germany to the Black Sea, has set successive records this summer for low water levels, threatening to shut down Hungary's only nuclear power plant, which uses water from the river to cool its reactors, for the first time in its 44-year history. Hungary's government has taken emergency interventions to raise the water level at the Paks plant, including sinking two 80-meter (262-foot) barges just upriver and beginning to install a riverbed sill designed to divert more water toward the plant's pumps. In such drought conditions, wetlands near rivers like the Danube normally act as a “natural reservoir” for retaining water when weather gets dry, said Ujj, the biodiversity specialist. The extremely low level of the Danube — as well as the increased chances for more frequent and intense floods — are effects of human-driven climate change that can be partially mitigated through appropriate land use and restoration of wetlands and other natural habitats, she added. “We do indeed expect water levels to fluctuate more, and we also expect precipitation patterns to become more extreme with drier summers,” she said. "However, restoring wetlands and increasing evaporation in certain areas could help boost precipitation during the summer months.”

DepEd: Nationwide school safety drill to push through Sept. 3. The National Simultaneous School Safety Drill will push through on Sept. 3 to strengthen schools’ preparedness for active threats, the Department of Education (DepEd) said on Tuesday, Sept. 1. In a statement, DepEd said the drill was rescheduled following consultations with the Philippine Psychiatric Association (PPA), Philippine Society for Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (PSCAP), and Philippine Pediatric Society (PPS) to ensure that safety protocols comply with child-centered, trauma-informed standards under its “Do No Harm” directive. According to DepEd Secretary Juan Edgardo “Sonny” Angara, efforts to ensure school safety must address both physical security and the mental well-being of learners. "Safety is not just about physical security; it is equally about protecting our children's peace of mind,” he said. Angara said DepEd is working closely with medical experts and psychiatric societies to keep children’s overall well-being at the center of the drill’s implementation. “Our goal for September 3 is to build calm operational confidence and muscle memory through proper orientation, not fear. Preparedness saves lives, and trauma-informed execution protects our learners," he added. DepEd said participating schools will prepare for the drill through teacher capacity-building, school readiness assessments, age-appropriate learner orientations, advance notices to learners, parents, and staff, and the securing of informed written parental consent and learner assent. “To build psychological readiness and eliminate surprise, school heads and teachers must provide advance notices to learners, parents, and staff. Schools are also required to secure informed written parental consent and learner assent before participation,” the agency said. “Learners identified as needing additional safeguards or whose parents request accommodations will be provided safe alternative activities without penalty or stigmatization,” it added. The education department said classes will conduct step-by-step walkthroughs of key protective measures, including securing entry points, remaining silent and out of sight of windows, and reviewing evacuation routes. Accommodations will be provided for learners with special needs, disabilities, or sensory sensitivities, it added. DepEd stressed that the drill will exclude all fear-inducing or graphic elements, including threat simulations, active aggressor role-players, weapon props, pyrotechnics, simulated gunfire, and artificial casualties, in accordance with existing disaster risk reduction guidelines. “Instead, a distinct signal separate from earthquake or fire alarms will initiate the activity. Schools will focus exclusively on building procedural muscle memory without generating distress,” it said. Angara said safety measures must be tailored to the varying levels of resilience and understanding among learners, as a one-size-fits-all approach would not address their individual needs. “When we prepare our learners and train our teachers with empathy, age-appropriate guidance, and proper care, we give our school communities confidence and reassurance instead of anxiety,” he said. “At the end of the day, our schools must remain sanctuaries where learners feel safe, supported, and protected at all times.” Per DepEd, designated guidance personnel and school health officers will provide psychological first aid (PFA) and conduct post-drill debriefings to maintain a supportive environment. “Schools will also establish clear referral arrangements with DepEd Schools Division Offices (SDOs), local government units (LGUs), and health facilities for learners needing specialized mental health care,” the agency said. As such, the education department said coordination with the Philippine National Police (PNP) will be limited to external perimeter security, emergency notification systems, dispatch response-time testing, and post-incident learner tracking. “Learners will also practice a compliance posture of raising hands high, empty and visible, upon encountering first responders during evacuation. Police officers are strictly prohibited from exposing learners to tactical disarming drills or aggressive uniform displays,” it stated. On Aug. 24, DepEd postponed the nationwide active attack simulation originally scheduled for Aug. 25 following concerns raised by the PPA and PSCAP. The groups cited insufficient evidence that such exercises reduce casualties and studies indicating that they could cause lasting psychological harm to learners.

Marcos to PCG: Always remember who you serve. President Marcos has reminded newly promoted flag officers of the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) to honor their oath and always remember who they serve. "Serve in a way that honors the oath that you took today. Lead with courage and integrity. Always remember who you serve," Marcos said in his speech. The President administered the oath of office to the newly promoted flag officers during a ceremony at Malacañan Palace on Tuesday, Sept. 1. He also urged them to lead by example and uphold the highest standard of integrity while preparing the next generation of Coast Guard leaders. "So to our newly promoted flag officers, lead by example, uphold the highest standards of integrity, prepare the next generation of Coast Guard leaders, embrace innovation and modernization, strengthen the partnerships that allow us to address challenges that no institution can tackle alone," he said. The Chief Executive underscored that the responsibility of the PCG is among the most crucial in government. "This past year alone has reminded us of that. Our Coast Guard has been out on the water patrolling the West Philippine Sea, escorting and supporting our re-provisioning missions there, and standing beside our fisherfolk in times of distress," Marcos said. The Coast Guard, Marcos further said, has also been keeping ports and travelers safe by inspecting vessels and looking after millions of passengers moving through the ports. It has protected the seas by conducting environmental inspections nationwide and the first responders when it comes to enforcing laws, such as going after illegal fishing, smuggling, and other threats. "Yesterday, we celebrated National Heroes Day. If there is one thing that this day reminds us, it is that courage is built long before the moment that it is tested. It is built through training, discipline, preparation, and the readiness to act when service calls for it," Marcos said. "This heroism is shown in the willingness to put the needs of others above your own, even when duty requires great personal risk. This is the courage that we see in the men and women of the Philippine Coast Guard. This is the standard that I ask you to carry into your command," Marcos added. The President also recognized the Coast Guard as it has always been present, rescuing families, and reaching communities that need help. "These are difficult, sometimes dangerous tasks. For these, we are all grateful for your sacrifice," he said.

MY OPPO App users had an additional layer of savings with a ₱2,000 voucher stackable on top of the base discount for the Reno16 F models through August 31. Flexible financing is widely available offline, offering up to 18-month 0% interest plans via Home Credit and up to 24-month 0% interest installments through major credit cards.

Japan Defense Ministry eyes record 8.9-T.-Yen budget for FY 2027. TOKYO, Aug. 31 (Jiji Press) -- Japan's Defense Ministry said Monday that it will ask for a record 8,890.8 billion yen under the government's budget for fiscal 2027, which starts next April. The figure is based on the existing Defense Buildup Program, which sets the country's defense spending at around 43 trillion yen for the five years through fiscal 2027. As the budget request includes many items for which specific amounts of necessary funds are not fixed yet, the total sum to be sought is likely to increase during the budget compilation process late this year. With the government planning to revise the country's three key security-related documents within this year to cover fiscal 2027 and later years, spending for many related measures in the budget request was left unspecified due to possible changes based on the document update. The fiscal 2027 budget request includes spending on measures featuring the use of artificial intelligence and drones in response to new warfare as a major pillar, as well as on organizational revamp plans, such as establishing a new agency to aid retired Self-Defense Forces members and their families. Specifically, the ministry will introduce AI to the SDF's Joint Operations Command in order to help commanding officers make swift decisions. It will utilize existing foreign AI systems for the time being while promoting the development of domestic systems. The ministry plans to introduce a high-security sovereign cloud as part of its AI platform. Utilizing private-sector technologies, the ministry will start developing long-range drones that can be mass-manufactured quickly and cheaply. It will also work on developing underwater-launched hypersonic guided missiles to enhance the country's standoff defense capabilities. Besides setting up the new agency for retired SDF members, which will have a staff of about 110, the ministry will establish three new bureaus, for international policies, defense infrastructure and facility policies. In light of Russia's prolonged invasion of Ukraine, the ministry will put efforts into securing sustained combat capabilities. As part of the move, it will begin research on introducing cargo ships equipped with autonomous navigation technology to ensure stable supplies of goods. Aiming to improve the country's defense equipment production bases, the ministry will newly set up an entity in charge of promoting exports of such equipment.

Gov’t explores cheaper feedstocks to raise bioethanol blend, cut fuel imports. The government is exploring cheaper feedstock sources as it looks to increase the country’s bioethanol blend and reduce dependence on imported fuel, according to the Department of Agriculture (DA). The DA said the government is studying the prospect of raising the bioethanol blend from 10 percent to 15 percent, or E10 to E15, in line with efforts to temper surging fuel prices in the domestic market. Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel said the increase would rely on cheaper and more diverse feedstock sources to also protect farmers and industries that depend on these resources. Tiu Laurel said the DA and the Department of Energy (DOE) are evaluating different feedstock options to support a higher bioethanol blend, including molasses, sugarcane juice, and corn. “We are studying these options carefully, and there is potential for them to help bring down gasoline prices,” said Tiu Laurel. Gasoline sold in the country is mandated to contain a locally sourced E10 blend to ensure a stable domestic market for locally produced feedstocks. A higher E20 blend is currently implemented on a voluntary basis. There are only nine petroleum stations that offer this bioethanol blend, based on estimates from the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA). Raising the current mandatory blend requires cheaper sources, as prices of sugarcane juice and molasses, which serve as the primary feedstocks, are usually double those of imported sources. The DA said locally sourced corn is the best candidate for an alternative feedstock to molasses and sugarcane, particularly in filling the current gap in local ethanol production. Domestic output from sugarcane-derived feedstock averages between 325 million and 385 million liters annually, while existing bioethanol plants have a capacity of more than 500 million liters. “To protect the sugarcane industry, only the unused capacity could be sourced from corn, which would accommodate additional production without displacing existing agricultural output,” the DA said. The agency said it would study expanded corn production through better seeds, mechanization, and contract farming between producers and ethanol plants to support this initiative. However, Tiu Laurel pointed out that the problem is not the availability of corn but whether it can be bought at a price that makes bioethanol commercially viable. The DA chief also said that higher demand for bioethanol could raise corn prices for livestock raisers, who depend on the crop for animal feed. As such, further diversifying feedstock sources is expected to reduce pressure on any single agricultural commodity and support stronger bioethanol production. Tiu Laurel said palm oil could become another long-term feedstock for biodiesel, although he noted that plantations take about three years to mature. Philippine Coconut Authority (PCA) Administrator and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Dexter Buted earlier told reporters that the government is also looking at increasing the country’s biodiesel blend by next year. Buted said this would hinge on whether prices of coco methyl ester (CME), which is used to produce biodiesel, would decline to a level that would not further raise petroleum prices. He said PCA has recommended hiking the biodiesel mandate from three percent to five percent, or B3 to B5, to the DOE.

LG unveils their evolution of an AI home at IFA 2026. LG is unveiling the next evolution of its AI Home at IFA 2026. Bringing together AI-powered appliances, connected services and contextual intelligence, LG AI Home simplifies daily routines, enhances convenience and delivers a more personalized and intuitive customer experience. A Home That Understands You LG AI Home analyzes schedules, routines, the home environment and appliance usage to recommend appropriate actions and optimize coordination between devices and services. By providing personalized suggestions based on real-world context, it proactively supports customers to spend less time managing their appliances and more time enjoying life. To illustrate this vision at IFA 2026, LG invites visitors to explore immersive AI Home spaces—spanning living, kitchen and rest zones—where they can experience firsthand how LG’s AI technologies coordinate devices and services around different everyday routines. ThinQ Claw: Extending AI Home Through Chat and Contextual Intelligence At IFA 2026, LG is introducing ThinQ Claw, a new text-chat-based AI agent experience that further enriches and expands the company’s AI Home offering. Built on the concept of OpenClaw and optimized specifically for LG AI Home, ThinQ Claw can understand user intent and context and help complete tasks by connecting and coordinating relevant services and devices. ThinQ Claw interprets updates shared by the user within the context of their life, rather than as isolated events. This enables it to recommend (or help initiate) appropriate actions aligned with personal preferences and the unique demands of each situation. It can manage cooking appliances to help the user prepare for hosting guests, monitor indoor air quality and temperature before the user arrives home to create a more comfortable environment based on current conditions, or suggest tailored experiences to entertain, empower or relax. Beyond appliance control, ThinQ Claw works collaboratively with daily services like calendars and other connected services. Instead of requiring complex automation rules, it allows users to share their plans or current status through a natural chat interface. In addition to being able to understand requests and determine the necessary steps, ThinQ Claw can remember customers’ likes and dislikes, leading to increasingly personalized experiences over time. This intelligent and context-aware agent expands how customers engage with AI Home by providing increasingly personalized support both inside and outside the home. ThinQ Claw will be demonstrated at LG’s AI Home Zone throughout IFA 2026. An Expanded AI Home Ecosystem The AI Home Zone highlights LG’s open AI Home ecosystem powered by Homey, a smart home platform developed by Athom, which LG acquired in 2024. With its broad interoperability across brands and connected devices, Homey enables a safe and reliable connected home experience. Homey allows users to manage diverse products from different manufacturers and service providers in one place. Through a comprehensive Home Energy Management System (HEMS) demonstration, IFA visitors can observe how Homey intelligently orchestrates energy generation, storage and consumption in real time by connecting smart meters, solar panels, home batteries and EV chargers with LG appliances. HEMS can help reduce household electricity bills by optimizing when energy is generated, stored and consumed, while taking advantage of dynamic energy pricing where supported.* IFA 2026 will also mark the European debut of LG ThinQ Pro. Designed for multi-family residential and commercial environments, ThinQ Pro supports the efficient management of devices and facilities while illustrating how LG’s AI Home vision extends beyond the home into shared and professional spaces. Applied across the entirety of the AI Home ecosystem, the LG Shield security framework helps protect connected appliances, services and customer data, enabling safe and secure AI experiences. “ThinQ Claw marks the next step in LG AI Home, illustrating how AI can understand customer intent and life context to support a more personalized and streamlined daily experience,” said Baek Seung-tae, president of the LG Home Appliance Solution Company. “LG will continue advancing AI Home through innovations that are increasingly intuitive and responsive to customers’ needs.”

Several Luzon areas get nearly 3 months’ worth of rain in August, says PAGASA. Several areas in Luzon recorded nearly three times their normal rainfall in August as heavy rains from the southwest monsoon or “habagat” contributed to unusually high monthly rainfall totals, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said. PAGASA weather specialist Benison Estareja said during a press conference on Tuesday, Sept. 1, that La Trinidad, Benguet recorded the highest accumulated rainfall in August at 2,868.7 millimeters from Aug. 1 to 31. The amount was equivalent to 298 percent of the station’s normal August rainfall of 963.3 millimeters. “Halos pang tatlong buwan na ulan yung inulan po sa La Trinidad Benguet for the month of August 2026 (La Trinidad, Benguet received nearly three months’ worth of rain in August 2026),” Estareja said. Iba, Zambales followed with 2,630 millimeters of rainfall from Aug. 1 to 31, equivalent to 284 percent of its normal August rainfall. Baguio City recorded 2,626.26 millimeters of rainfall for the month, compared with its normal August rainfall of 963.2 millimeters. This was equivalent to 273 percent of normal. The figures showed that Iba and Baguio City also received nearly three times their normal August rainfall, Estareja said. Abucay, Bataan recorded 2,210 millimeters of rainfall, placing it among the top five stations with the highest rainfall totals for August. However, no comparison with its normal August rainfall was available because it is a new PAGASA station. Olongapo City, meanwhile, logged 2,100 millimeters, or 243 percent of its normal August rainfall. Although not part of the top five, the PAGASA Science Garden monitoring station in Quezon City also recorded a significant amount of rainfall at 1,510 millimeters for the month. This was equivalent to 266 percent of its normal August rainfall of 568.5 millimeters. “Nakakontribute po yung ganito karaming ulan na 1,500 millimeters nung August 8, nung August 17, nung August 29 (The rainfall amounting to 1,500 millimeters was contributed by the rains on Aug. 8, Aug. 17, and Aug. 29),” he said.

Japan govt asks eastern city to accept N-waste site survey. HITACHIOMIYA, Ibaraki Pref., Aug. 31 (Jiji Press) -- The industry ministry on Monday asked the city of Hitachiomiya in Ibaraki Prefecture, eastern Japan, to accept a literature survey for selecting a final disposal site for high-level radioactive waste from nuclear power plants. If realized, Hitachiomiya would become the fifth site in the country to accept a literature survey, after the town of Suttsu and the village of Kamoenai, both in the northernmost prefecture of Hokkaido, the town of Genkai in the southwestern prefecture of Saga and Minamitorishima, a remote Tokyo island in the Ogasawara chain in the Pacific. This is the second case of the central government seeking approval for the literature survey without a request from local communities. Senior ministry officials visited Hitachiomiya and handed a written request to Mayor Sadayuki Suzuki. "I view the request very positively," the mayor said, adding that he wants to make a final decision after hearing from the city assembly. Industry minister Ryosei Akazawa later told reporters at his ministry in Tokyo that he is grateful to Suzuki for taking the state's request seriously. "The government will take the initiative in approaching other municipalities to expand the areas subject to literature surveys," he added. Hitachiomiya is located in the northwestern part of Ibaraki and borders Tochigi Prefecture. The city was included in the scientific features map released by the central government in 2017, which listed sites where the possibility of favorable features to host a final disposal facility, such as no volcanoes or active faults nearby, being found is relatively high. Although Hitachiomiya is landlocked, parts of the city are located some 20 kilometers to the coast, making it favorable from a transportation perspective as well. The literature survey, the first stage of the three-tier selection process, is aimed at examining the possible effects of volcanoes and faults based on geological maps and scientific papers over a period of about two years. The consent of the prefectural governor and the heads of relevant municipalities is required to proceed to the second and third stages--preliminary and detailed investigations. The overall selection process is said to take a total of some 20 years. Ibaraki Governor Kazuhiko Oigawa said he will "closely watch" how the city of Hitachiomiya will respond.

Sotto: No person behind alias? Then, it's a 'fake name'. Senator-judge Vicente "Tito" Sotto III on Tuesday, Sept. 1, clarified that Philippine law allows the use of pseudonyms only for specific literary and entertainment purposes, distinguishing these from fictitious or fake names. Sotto made the clarification during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, citing Republic Act No. 6085, the law regulating the use of aliases. “The general rule, Mr. President, that she mentioned is Republic Act 6085, regulating the use of aliases. It's only allowed in the Philippines only for pseudonyms, solely for literary, cinema, television and other entertainment purposes,” Sotto said. Sotto said the existence of a real person behind a name determines whether it is an alias. “If there is a person behind the alias, then it is an alias,” he said. “If there is no person behind the name, it is a fictitious name or a fake name,” he added. Sotto made the manifestation after reviewing the impeachment court's journal concerning the previous trial's questioning of private prosecutor Mae Divinagracia by Senator-judge Robin Padilla. He said he wanted to clarify the matter after seeing a newspaper report stating that Divinagracia had been prevented from answering and had been cut off several times. Sotto said the journal showed that Divinagracia was able to answer most of Padilla's questions, although there were one or two instances when she was cut off. He said Divinagracia was discussing RA 6085 when she was interrupted and that the court allowed her to answer, although she was unable to elaborate further. Sotto said he was making the clarification “just for the record” and for the information of the public and members of the impeachment court. Presiding Officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero acknowledged Sotto's manifestation.

Japan FY 2027 budget requests likely to top 143 trillion Yen. TOKYO, Aug. 31 (Jiji Press) -- General-account budget requests from Japanese government agencies and ministries for fiscal 2027 are expected to exceed 143 trillion yen, hitting a record high for the fourth consecutive year. The figure will be much higher than the 122,445.4 billion yen sought under the government's fiscal 2026 general-account budget. On Monday, the Finance Ministry finished accepting budget requests for the fiscal year starting in April 2027. The anticipated increase in the total requested amount reflects the government's decision to include funds for measures that have been earmarked under supplementary budgets in the initial budget and create a new investment quota with no caps set on the amounts to be sought. The new quota will be for investments in the crisis management and growth fields to create a strong and prosperous Japan. Also, ministries and agencies were allowed to make fund requests without setting specific amounts for certain measures. Fund requests for the new investment quota topped 10 trillion yen, the level assumed by the government in its estimates. The industry ministry made the largest request of 4,525 billion yen. Debt-servicing costs will likely balloon due to an increase in coupon payments reflecting rising interest rates. As a result, the overall budget request for fiscal 2027 is expected to go up by over 2 pct from 140,612.6 billion yen, the combined amount of the fiscal 2026 initial budget and the fiscal 2025 supplementary budget. The health ministry made a record budget request totaling 36,580.3 billion yen. While the size of the Defense Ministry's latest budget request is almost the same as that for the previous year, many of its requests did not show specific amounts as the government is set to update the country's three major national security documents later this year. The Finance Ministry plans to secure a record 36,638.6 billion yen to cover debt-servicing costs in fiscal 2027, up by 5,362.8 billion yen from fiscal 2026. The growth reflects a hike in the assumed long-term interest rate to 3.8 pct from 3.0 pct. Voicing plans to strictly scrutinize the submitted requests, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said at a press conference Tuesday last week that the requested funds "should naturally contribute to growth or induce private investments." "We hope to build a strong economy and realize fiscal sustainability at the same time in an integrated way under our responsible and proactive fiscal policy," she said.

JBC invites 5 SC senior justices to apply for Chief Justice post to be vacated by Gesmundo on Nov. 6. The Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) has invited the five senior associate justices of the Supreme Court (SC) to apply for the Chief Justice post that would be vacated on November 6 with the compulsory retirement of Chief Justice Alexander G. Gesmundo. In a message to journalists, SC Spokesperson Atty. Camille Sue Mae L. Ting said that those invited by the JBC were Senior Associate Justice Marvic M.V.F. Leonen and Associate Justices Alfredo Benjamin S. Caguioa, Ramon Paul L. Hernando, Henri Jean Paul B. Inting, and Rodil V. Zalameda. It was presumed that since Associate Justice Amy C. Lazaro-Javier – who is currently the fourth senior associate justice -- is compulsory retiring at age 70 on November 16, she was no longer invited to apply and her place was given to Associate Justice Zalameda. The five associate justices may apply or may be nominated. However, they have the option to decline the nomination. Ting said that “since the early 2000s, the JBC has followed the practice of inviting the five most senior associate justices to apply for the Chief Justice post as a matter of courtesy and in recognition of their seniority.” “What has begun as an informal practice has since become a standing JBC policy,” he also said. The deadline for the submission of the application or nomination for the Chief Justice post will be at 4:30 p.m. on October 13. Applicants or those who will submit nominations must visit the JBC website – www.jbc.judiciary.gov.ph – for the complete details and guidelines. Under Section 7, Article VII of the Constitution, a member of the SC – including the Chief Justice – must be a natural-born citizen, at least 40 years of age, and has served as a lower court judge or practiced law in the Philippines for 15 years or more. He or she must be a person of proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence. The JBC -- the constitutional office that accepts, screens, and nominates appointments to the judiciary, the Office of the Ombudsman and its deputies, and members of the Legal Education Board – is mandated to submit at least three nominees to President Marcos for appointment. Whoever is appointed by the President would be his second appointment to the SC. His first appointee is Associate Justice Raul B. Villanueva. If the President has not appointed Gesmundo’s replacement after the submission of the JBC’s nominees, Senior Associate Justice Leonen will be acting Chief Justice starting November 6.
